passage: Every night that week, Nkechi said the same thing in their shared kitchen in Leeds: "Tomorrow I'm starting the dissertation proposal. First thing." And every next evening Yara found her on the sofa, laptop closed, looking more tired than before. By Thursday Nkechi wasn't even saying tomorrow. She just stirred her noodles and said, "I'm hopeless." Yara thought about the pep talks she had tried, which hadn't helped. So instead she carried her own laptop to the table. "Twenty minutes. I'll do my reading, you do the easiest bit. Just the title page, maybe the reference list." Nkechi hesitated, then opened the file. Twenty minutes later she had a title, three references and half a sentence. She didn't stop at twenty. Yara pretended not to notice.

qa.q: What did Yara suggest Nkechi do in the twenty minutes?
qa.a: The easiest bit: just the title page, maybe the reference list.

qa.q: What does Nkechi's "I'm hopeless" suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: Each broken promise to start tomorrow has added shame, so she now sees herself as the problem, which makes starting feel even harder.

qa.q: Which choice of Yara's worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting down beside Nkechi for a short, fixed time with the easiest piece; it swapped pressure for company and made the first step small enough to take.

qa.q: How does Yara see the week, and why does she stop giving pep talks?
qa.a: Yara watches her friend grow more tired and self-critical each evening, sees the pep talks aren't helping, and switches to quietly working beside her.

Dear Vijay,
I'm writing this instead of saying it, because saying it might feel like a lecture, and you've had enough of those. For three weeks I've heard you say, "Tomorrow I start revising for the backlog paper." And each time tomorrow comes and goes, you seem a bit smaller. Last Sunday you said you're just not made for this. I don't believe that. I think the paper has grown so big in your head that every start looks like a mountain. So here's my offer: Wednesday, 4 p.m., the second-floor reading room. Twenty minutes, both of us. You pick the easiest chapter, the one on definitions, and I'll do my own work next to you. If you want to leave after twenty, leave. No questions.
Your friend,
Preeti

Week one, a Monday. In the reading room, Pallavi pushed her thesis folder away. "I'll start the literature review tomorrow, properly." Madhuri nodded and kept working, but noticed Pallavi's jaw was tight.

Week two, a Thursday. Same words, softer. "Tomorrow, promise." This time Pallavi left early, and later sent Madhuri a message: "I'm useless." Madhuri read it three times, a knot in her stomach, and replied with a heart.

Week three, a Tuesday. Madhuri waited by the library steps. "Sit with me for twenty minutes," she said. "Just twenty. What's the easiest piece?" Pallavi thought. "Listing the papers I've already read." They sat side by side, Madhuri on her own work, Pallavi typing titles. When the timer went off, Pallavi had a list of eleven and didn't stop. Madhuri pretended not to notice the smile.

passage: Come, sit, I'll tell you about Arnab. We were in the same hostel in Shillong, both doing botany, when I was about your age. Every evening in the mess, Arnab said the same thing: "From tomorrow I'll start the herbarium file." The next evening, again tomorrow. I noticed he ate less each time he said it, and once he just stared at his plate and said, "What's wrong with me?" I felt sorry and also a little annoyed, I won't pretend. I didn't know what to do. Then one night I said, "Arnab, bring your file. We'll sit in the common room for twenty minutes. Just press one leaf." He came, grumbling. That leaf became six. In the end he submitted before me. So when you watch a friend going round and round, remember that, beta. Lalremsiami learned it at nineteen.

passage:
My friend Zainab has been “starting tomorrow” on her dissertation proposal for three weeks. I'm Jyoti; we share a room in the hostel.
Every night she'd say, “Tomorrow, first thing.” Every next night she'd be quieter, more tired, scrolling in the dark. On Thursday she said, “I'm such a failure,” and I felt something twist in my chest. She's not. She's the smartest person I know.
So on Friday morning I put my laptop next to hers and said, “Twenty minutes. I'll work on my stuff, you just write the title and three possible research questions. Bad ones are fine.”
She laughed a little. She wrote the title. Then the three questions. Then she added a fourth.
When the timer rang, she didn't stop.
That night she didn't say “tomorrow.” She said, “I'll do the literature bit after breakfast.” That sounded different.

qa.a: Jyoti felt something twist inside, hurt and worried for a friend Jyoti sees as very smart.

Week 6. Hansa, my mentee from the English batch, told me on Monday she would start the literature essay "tomorrow for sure." She said the same thing last Monday and the Monday before.
Each time she says it, she looks a little more tired. Today she admitted she hadn't slept well because she kept thinking about the essay. "I'm just the kind of person who can't start," she said. That worried me more than the essay.
I didn't lecture. I asked if she'd sit with me in the common room for twenty minutes, phones away, and do only the easiest bit, the title and three quotes she liked.
She agreed, a bit reluctantly. After twenty minutes she had the title, four quotes and one rough sentence. She laughed and said, "That's more than two weeks."
We'll do the same on Thursday.

14 October, night
Deepika said it again today at lunch: "I'll start the lab report tomorrow, pakka." I, Lakshmi, have heard "pakka" from her four times now.
The strange part is that she looks worse each time. Today she barely touched her rajma. She said, "I'm so useless, I don't know what's wrong with me." I didn't know what to say, and I felt awful, because I've done this too, with my thesis outline last year.
So after dinner I knocked on her door and said, "Twenty minutes. I'll sit here with my own notes. You just do the easiest part."
She chose the aim and the list of apparatus. Took her ten minutes. Then she kept going for another half hour, and I pretended to read.
When I left she said thank you twice. Tomorrow, same time. Pakka.

qa.q: How many times has Lakshmi heard Deepika say "pakka"?
qa.a: Lakshmi has heard it four times now.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when Deepika called herself useless?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt awful and unsure what to say, partly because Lakshmi had done the same thing with a thesis outline last year.

qa.q: What made Lakshmi's offer helpful?
qa.a: Offering to sit nearby for twenty minutes and start with the easiest part made beginning feel small and supported, which got Deepika going.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel at the end of the evening?
qa.a: Deepika probably feels relieved and grateful, saying thank you twice after finally making real progress.

In the small college town of Hoshangabad, Pankaj and Mohit shared a rented room above a tailor's shop. For three weeks Pankaj had watched the same thing: every night Mohit said, "Tomorrow I'll start the project report, for sure," and every next night he said it again, a little quieter, and went to bed looking more miserable.
On Friday Mohit didn't even say it. He just lay facing the wall.
Pankaj pulled his chair up to Mohit's bed. "Twenty minutes. I'll sit with you. We don't write the report. We just do the easiest bit. The title page."
"That's stupid. That's nothing."
"Exactly. Nothing is easy to start."
Mohit laughed despite himself. They did the title page. Then, since the laptop was open anyway, the contents list. When Pankaj's alarm rang after twenty minutes, Mohit said, "Five more."
